items.title: Mortgage and Loan Insurance Programs Under the National Housing Act-Debenture Interest Rates
items.summary: This notice announces changes in the interest rates to be paid on debentures issued with respect to a loan or mortgage insured by the Federal Housing Administration under the provisions of the National Housing Act (the Act). The interest rate for debentures issued under Section 221(g)(4) of the Act during the 6-month period beginning January 1, 2026, is 4 percent. The interest rate for debentures issued under any other provision of the Act is the rate in effect on the date that the commitment to insure the loan or mortgage was issued, or the date that the loan or mortgage was endorsed (or initially endorsed if there are two or more endorsements) for insurance, whichever rate is higher. The interest rate for debentures issued under these other provisions with respect to a loan or mortgage committed or endorsed during the 6-month period beginning January 1, 2026, is 4\3/4\ percent.

This supplemental notice of proposed rulemaking continues HUD's efforts to remove or revise regulations that prohibit conduct having a disparate impact without evidence of discriminatory intent. Through this rule, HUD is proposing to remove provisions in HUD's Title VI implementing regulations that impose disparate-impact liability on recipients of HUD Federal financial assistance. items.summary: New data from the Federal Trade Commission reveal that people reported losing a staggering $3.5 billion to imposter scams in 2025, with reported losses increasing nearly three times since 2020. FTC data also show that people reported imposter scams more than any other fraud category in 2025—nearly one in three fraud reports were about imposter scams. These scams lured consumers through text, phone, email, social media, search engine results and other means. trends_raw:
Volume held nearly flat, 169 evidence candidates against 170 on 09/03/26, with nothing surfacing for the first time in this run. That makes this a consolidation day rather than a break day, and it puts the emphasis on which beats are accumulating rather than which are spiking. Housing and financial security each added an item; long-term care and Medicare and Medicaid each shed one. Medicare and Medicaid remains the heaviest beat at 29 items, followed by long-term care at 18, housing at 14, workforce at 12, financial security at 11 and palliative and hospice care at 9.

The shape matters more than the counts. Medicare and Medicaid is the busiest beat but it is not one story — cohesion sits at 0.054 across seven sources ranging from CMS provider files to Federal Register notices on the RAPID device coverage pathway and KFF data notes on Medicaid coverage for women and rural maternity access. Those items share a tag and nothing else. The same holds for housing at 0.031, financial security at 0.048, caregiving at 0.031 and workforce at 0.096. Only three clusters actually hold together: palliative and hospice care at 0.457, long-term care at 0.256 and depression and mental health at 0.112.

Coverage posture is the run's real signal. There are 84 confirmed gaps, meaning monitored publishers work those beats and none matched the item, and 76 items on beats where no monitored publisher is watching at all. Within the long-term care cluster, 17 of 18 items are unmatched; the palliative and hospice cluster is unmatched on all nine. The freshest material is regulatory and local — the Housing Trust Fund allocation notice and the American Community Survey state aging and housing profile both sit at zero days old, and 15 of the 18 long-term care items break below the national level, most of them to states and counties. The opportunity in this run is geographic specificity, not speed.ack: the federal files are public and static, so the win goes to whoever localizes them first.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** On 08/01/26 CMS refreshed essentially the entire public record on nursing homes at once — Provider Information, Ownership, Penalties, Health Deficiencies, Fire Safety Deficiencies, Survey Summary, Inspection Dates, MDS Quality Measures, Medicare Claims Quality Measures, the Skilled Nursing Facility Quality Reporting Program file, Nursing Home Data Collection Intervals and the Citation Code Look-up, with Facility Affiliation Data on 07/31/26, Patient-Reported Outcomes on 08/05/26 and Utilization Data on 08/11/26. What connects them is not that they arrived together but what they now measure against: BLS puts nursing care facilities employment at 1,590.20 thousand jobs in August 2026, up 2.1% year over year, while home health care services employment sits at 1,896.40 thousand, up 5.0%. The staffing that drives the Five-Star Rating System is growing at less than half the rate of the home-based alternative, and Justice in Aging's 08/20/26 primer on Medicaid Home and Community-Based Services documents the policy gaps that limit access to that alternative. The Center for Retirement Research's 09/03/26 comparison of long-term care in Israel and the United States frames the same bind as structural rather than local. So the facility scorecard has a new edition, the workforce behind the ratings is thinning relative to home care, and the escape route from facility care is documented as rationed. This cluster coheres at 0.256 across four independent sources, 17 of its 18 items unmatched by monitored publishers.

**Why pitch this now:** The federal calendar turns on October 1. HUD published FY 2027 Fair Market Rents on 09/01/26 and the Housing Trust Fund FY 2026 allocation notice on 09/04/26, both of which reset what subsidized housing costs and where the money goes for the coming year. Families weighing a nursing home this fall are doing it against a citation record that now covers a fresh three-year window, and against a home care labor market that is pulling workers in the other direction.

**Angle:** "The New Nursing Home Report Card, County by County" — a data-driven consumer guide built from the refreshed CMS provider files, showing how to read penalties, ownership and staffing for a specific facility, paired with the BLS staffing trend that explains why the numbers look the way they do. Written for adult children shortlisting facilities in the next 90 days, with a companion trade read for operators on where the labor is going.

**Potential headlines:**
- The nursing home inspection record just refreshed. Here is how to read yours.
- Nursing home staffing grew 2.1 percent. Home health grew 5 percent.
- What the new CMS penalty and ownership files say about the home down the road

**Potential outlets:**
- Seniors Guide — Tier 1 consumer senior living, and the facility-shortlisting reader is exactly its audience.
- SeniorLiving.org — Tier 2 consumer resource built around comparison tools, a natural home for a county-level read of the CMS files.
- McKnight's Long-Term Care News — Tier 1 long-term care trade, the outlet whose readers own the citation and penalty numbers.
- Home Health Care News — Tier 1 home care trade, and the 5.0% employment growth figure is a home care story before it is a facility story.
- Senior Housing News — Tier 1 senior living trade, for the ownership and affiliation data angle.
pitch_ideas_raw:
**CMS nursing home file refresh (08/01/26, 07/31/26, 08/05/26, 08/11/26, score 69–73, confirmed gap, breaks to states and counties).** **For readers:** Before you tour anything, pull the Provider Information file for the homes on your list and check three things — certified bed count, the staffing measures used in the Five-Star Rating System, and the quality measure scores. Then pull Penalties for fines and payment denials in the last three years, Health Deficiencies and Fire Safety Deficiencies for the actual citations with their scope and severity, and Ownership to see who runs the place now. The Citation Code Look-up translates the tag numbers into plain descriptions, so you can ask an admissions director about a specific citation instead of a general worry. **For the trade:** The Facility Affiliation Data and Ownership files, read together across a market, show which chains are consolidating and how affiliation tracks with citation counts. Operators should assume referral sources and family decision-makers are working from the same refreshed three-year citation window and prepare a plain-language response to each open tag.

**BLS employment and wage series, August 2026 and July 2026 (score 63–68, confirmed gap).** **For readers:** If a facility tells you staffing is stable, the national picture says the sector is growing slowly — nursing care facilities at 1,590.20 thousand jobs, up 2.1% year over year, and continuing care retirement communities and assisted living at 1,026.90 thousand, up 1.4%. Home health care services grew 5.0% to 1,896.40 thousand jobs. Ask any community you are considering for its own turnover and agency-staffing numbers, and ask whether home-based care could cover what you need instead. **For the trade:** Assisted living and CCRC average hourly earnings hit $25.65 in July 2026, up 3.2%, while home health care services pay $28.04, up 2.0%. Congregate settings are raising wages faster and still paying less per hour than the home-based competitor that is growing employment two and a half times as fast. That is a recruiting math problem, not a marketing one.

**CMS hospice CAHPS survey data, national and state (08/07/26, score 72, confirmed gap).** **For readers:** Hospice choice is usually made in a hurry, which is why the state-level CAHPS averages matter — they let you see how families in your state rate Medicare-certified hospice providers before you sign anything, and they give you a benchmark to hold a specific agency against. **For the trade:** The palliative and hospice cluster is the most coherent in this run at 0.457 cohesion, drawing on CMS provider data and RAND research across nine items, none of them matched by a monitored publisher. Providers should expect the state comparison to become the reference point in referral conversations.

**HUD Fair Market Rents for FY 2027 (09/01/26) and Housing Trust Fund FY 2026 allocation notice (09/04/26, score 63 and 67, confirmed gap).** **For readers:** Fair Market Rents are adjusted to take effect October 1, and they set what a Housing Choice Voucher covers where you live. If you rent on a fixed income, check the FY 2027 figure for your area now rather than after a lease renewal, and note that public housing agencies can request reevaluations under the Housing Opportunity Through Modernization Act of 2016. **For the trade:** The Housing Trust Fund allocation notice names the 50 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, American Samoa, Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands as eligible grantees, which is the affordable senior housing pipeline for the coming year.

**Medicaid HCBS primer from Justice in Aging (08/20/26) alongside KFF's provider tax brief (08/20/26) and Medicaid/CHIP enrollment tracker (08/26/26, score 57–58, confirmed gap).** **For readers:** If staying home is the goal, the HCBS primer lays out how Medicaid home and community-based services support independent living and where access breaks down. Find out whether your state has a waiting list and what the functional eligibility screen actually asks. **For the trade:** KFF's brief draws on its 2025-2026 survey of Medicaid directors and a proposed rule to describe how provider tax rules are changing under the 2025 reconciliation law and the regulations implementing it, and which states each change may affect. Anyone modeling Medicaid revenue for 2027 needs that state-by-state read.

**CMS Medical Equipment Suppliers refresh (08/30/26, score 74, the highest-scoring item this run, confirmed gap, breaks to states and counties).** **For readers:** The supplier file lists what each location carries and its Medicare participation status. Before you order a walker, a hospital bed or oxygen, confirm the supplier's participation status, because that is what determines what you pay out of pocket.
